item.title: Surrendering Control When a Loved One's Health Declines
item.description:
Grief

Surrendering Control When a Loved One's Health Declines

Why we try to control the uncontrollable, and how we can start to let go.

Posted September 27, 2026

Key points
  • Many who grew up in dysfunctional families rely on control as a go-to coping tool.
  • Control over other peoples’ lives is usually an illusion.
  • For the adult child of a parent or loved one in severe health decline, letting go of control may be healthy.
  • Tools such as positive reappraisal or saying the Serenity Prayer may assist in this situation.
Source: LabRobotUIGear/Leonardo.AI

For those of us who grew up in dysfunctional and/or chaotic households, control may have been a tool we used to cope with the uncontrollable. However, as you probably know, the belief that we can control everything is just an illusion to calm our stressed-out nervous systems.

This coping method may begin to fall apart when we realize the limit to the amount of control we have in our lives. While certain coping tools may assist us in surviving a chaotic childhood, they may be more detrimental to our well-being as adults.

I understand wanting an ordered, predictable life. Heck, I used to be the queen of wanting predictability.

At a certain point, though, we realize that the concentric circles of what are under our control are actually much smaller than we’d thought. Attempting to control that which we cannot control can only lead to frustration and a lack of inner peace, forever chasing the unattainable.

Trying to Control the Uncontrollable When a Loved One Falls Ill

Surviving a loved one with a terminal illness or an elderly parent in severe health decline is a perfect example of this. Emotionally gutting, at times it saps every ounce of our emotional energy. Knowing the inevitable is coming for the parent or loved one and not having any genuine control over it can feel like standing in a house with a shaky foundation, awaiting the big earthquake.

It may also place us in a holding pattern, not sure of how or when to proceed with important aspects of our lives for fear of the loved one’s health taking a drastic downturn. For those who have lived with this situation for a long time, there may be a feeling of—and guilt over—just wondering when the emotional exhaustion will be over and the inevitable tragic ending will occur. These are all natural feelings for a deeply painful experience for which we cannot control.

How to Start Letting Go of the Illusion of Control

Letting go of the belief that we can control the situation, though, may be an essential ingredient in maintaining emotional well-being in this circumstance. This is especially true when control is often what we want most for our declining loved one’s health.

1. Finding inner peace by changing our cognitions: "Secondary control strategy"

One strategy for releasing control may be attempting to change one’s own cognitions about the situation (referred to as a "secondary control strategy") rather than trying to change the loved one’s health situation itself ("primary control strategy"), such as in the case of caring for a parent with dementia.

Secondary control strategies such as positive reappraisal (reframing the situation to find the positive aspect or any possible "silver lining") may be more effective than primary control strategies in this circumstance. While it may be difficult to find a silver lining in this case, an example might be thinking tenderly about happy memories with the parent or loved one, as well as spending more frequent and quality time with them, even when it is over the phone or video chat.

2. Remind yourself that it's not a linear process.

Letting go is far from a linear process, though. It’s more akin to a push-pull of anticipatory grief over the impending loss, followed by attempts at letting go, and then wanting to pull the loved one back to us emotionally again. The mind and brain know we need to let go, but the heart and soul want desperately to hold onto our loved one.

This push-pull process of letting go may be eased a bit for some individuals through spiritual coping methods. For those who resonate with spiritual coping methods, saying the Serenity Prayer may assist them in letting go of control and may provide feelings of comfort.

3. Remember: It is their path, not ours.

A certain amount of relief may also come with the realization and acceptance that it is the parent or relative’s path to travel and not ours. Our path includes supporting and assisting them when we can while taking care of our own emotional, physical and spiritual well-being, and knowing when to let go of the illusion of control.

Above all, though, remember to be gentle with yourself while attempting to let go. Self-care is vital on this tender journey.

item.title: 3 Ways to Use AI to Improve Your Cognitive Flexibility and Sharpness
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

3 Ways to Use AI to Improve Your Cognitive Flexibility and Sharpness

You don't have to care about efficiency or productivity to value growth.

Posted September 27, 2026

Source: AI generated image; Google Gemini

Ruth is not interested in optimization in the tech-bro sense, but she is interested in growth. She knows she feels better when she has a sense that she is quietly improving her cognitive sharpness and emotional resilience.

Over her life and career, she has done this through approaching the everyday challenges of life responsibly and conscientiously. Now, somewhat reluctantly, she has been wondering if AI has something to offer her in improving her thinking and skills.

On one hand, she has some ethical objections to AI and hates the sense of pressure to use it for fear of getting left behind. On the other, she has some curiosity about whether it has something positive to offer her.

This article is for someone like Ruth who is curious but hesitant about AI, who values a sense of being strong and capable, and who likes to approach personal growth gently and creatively rather than from a place of urgency or self-criticism.

How to Use AI to Make Your Own Thinking Sharper

People mostly think about using AI for cognitive off-loading of thinking rigor and responsibility. But that doesn't have to be how you use it. It can also be a tool for cognitively and emotionally challenging yourself.

1. Use AI to Gain Awareness of Ways You Don’t Naturally Think

We all have thinking strengths, which can become narrower and more specialized over time. We tend to take the same approach to problem-solving, no matter what the problem. We tend to use the same tools, resources, and mental shortcuts.

When our thinking strengths (like care and caution) are rewarded with success, or we feel a sense they're protecting us from harm, we double down on those.

Exploring topics and tasks via AI can help you see approaches and tools you don’t even think of. This surfacing of what we don’t know we don't know (including about our ways of operating and alternative tools or perspectives we never would have thought of) is one of the most valuable uses of AI for ordinary people.

2. Use AI to Become More Open to Taking Advice

Most people are more receptive to advice they ask for and have ample time and space to process than unsolicited advice. I've found that AI can help you peacefully explore areas where you have some psychological resistance, avoidance, or fear. For example, you might talk to it about your hesitation about making a will (of course, all the usual caveats apply about not relying on it being right).

The fact that many AI programs save each conversation separately allows you to pick up a topic weeks or months later, when you have the mental space to explore it, or it reaches the top of your priority list (for example, finances and investing topics). This can allow you to get aspects of your life in order at your own pace, and give you all the time and space you need to mull over various options.

3. Use AI to Find Examples of Thinking That Inspire You

I spend a lot of time asking AI to find examples of creative thinking, like people who see workarounds to barriers when most other people would just see the barrier.

My favorite ways to do this are by asking AI to analyze YouTube videos (e.g., long-form interviews) or, for example, dump the data from years of a question-and-answer forum into AI, and then query it.

To identify creative thinking in others, I ask a lot of questions that contain terms like creative, under-the-radar, unusual, long-tail strengths, assumptions, barriers, resilience, tools, and resources.

Know When AI Is Most Likely to Give You Sophisticated Ideas

When using AI for these purposes, consider what data it has been trained on. It’s probably going to be much better at helping you learn new approaches related to topics like tech and finance that are more objective and that have highly structured documentation than emotional topics, where most of its training data will tend to be broader concepts you’ve probably heard a lot about before already.

Let Your Own Values Guide Your Growth

You don’t need to adopt the values of AI companies to benefit from their tools. You can not care about efficiency or productivity, but still use the tools to support your own values and priorities.

item.title: The Trap of Measuring Your Success on External Achievements
item.description:
Self-Esteem

The Trap of Measuring Your Success on External Achievements

When self-worth relies on external validation, the finish line will only move further away.

Posted September 27, 2026

Key points
  • Overly relying on external validation could cause you to feel you need to keep chasing achievements.
  • It's important for you to be able to internally validate yourself.
  • You don't always need to be achieving things to be worthwhile.

Reinforcement shapes our behavior. The society you live in and the people around you impact what you perceive as good behavior (e.g. graduating from school, getting a job, etc.). You are more likely to repeat a behavior when you receive praise and appreciation (e.g. a sticker, a smile, a "thank you,"). These are forms of external validation.

The Risk of Relying on External Validation

External validation isn't inherently a bad thing. Nevertheless, it can get you into trouble if you find yourself relying on the validation of the people and world around you as the only way you can identify your success and worth. This can put you at risk of creating a cycle of doing things for the external reinforcement you may achieve, rather than the internal validation you generate (such as feelings of growth and satisfaction from your effort).

Notice if external achievements (e.g. getting praise from others, receiving recognition) has become the primary way you gauge if you are "good enough."

This theme comes up often in my work with professional women and high achievers in general. And the truth is that a drive to gain external reinforcement can get you pretty far in life. Maybe it helped you do well in school (including graduate school). It might have motivated you to engage in athletic, volunteer, and vocational activities and keep going, even if you didn't really enjoy the activity, because of the recognition you received (or were trying to receive).

Being involved in such activities and earning achievements may have been your go-to way of getting praise from those around you or the way that you avoided being punished (emotionally, mentally, or physically) by parental figures. You may feel like you always need to be chasing approval and validation from others if that has been you default model.

Source: Fil Hernandez / Unsplash

When Will You Know When You've Done Enough?

The older you get in life, there are fewer structured opportunities for external validation. You may have a performance review once a year, rather than be getting grades every week. The feedback, if it's thoughtful, will also usually be nuanced and mixed with things you are doing well and things that could be better.

You may make it to the top of your profession and feel like you have nowhere to grow or feel empty inside if it doesn't come with consistent, positive, external validation. If you are relying on external validation alone to inform you of how you are doing, then it might feel overly impactful and/or it may be hard to not feel shaken by any data that seems critical or negative.

You may also notice that you have difficulty actually feeling the positive emotions from your achievements, or that the feelings are fleeting, as if you need to immediately pursue the next goal. Therefore, continuing to rely on external evaluation can get you into trouble if you don't have a comparable way to internally motivate, reinforce, and value yourself.

Find Ways to Internally Validate Yourself

Even if you do everything "right" the people around you may not be able or willing to provide you with the validation you crave. Or their validation may include some negative feedback, which could lead you to discount the positive. It's important to find ways to validate yourself, to intentionally identify the intent and effort you put into your actions, and not discount the positive. These tips can help:

1. Speak to yourself kindly.

You can be your worst critic, your biggest cheerleader, and sometimes both. Be mindful of how you speak to yourself, as your thoughts shape how you view yourself, others, and the world.

Over the next week, intentionally notice and log the negative things you say to yourself. If you make a mistake is your accompanying automatic thought something like "of course I messed up" or "I'll never be as good as them." Such thoughts are filled with unhelpful thinking traps that are important to recognize and reframe.

  • Instead of "of course I messed up" a more fair thought would be "I made a mistake, all humans do. What can I learn from this?"
  • Instead of "I'll never be as good as them" a more balanced thought could be "Comparing myself to them isn't productive. How have I improved over the past few months, and how can I continuing my own development?"

2. Intentionally identify your intent and effort.

Rather can relying on external validation (i.e. reinforcement from others) give credence to your internal positive intentions and the effort you put into what you do. You could say and do all the "perfect" things and the person you are interacting with still may not care or provide you with reinforcement. If you are relying on that external feedback you could be discounting the positive things you are doing.

Shift your focus from relying on external validation to instead giving yourself encouragement and praise. It's still valid to integrate external feedback into how you view your performance, however it needs to be considered as only one portion of the equation of how you view yourself and your success.

3. Don't discount the positive.

Finally, don't discount the positive. Your efforts are still meaningful, even if you don't get first place, a perfect score, or the promotion.

Imagine telling an Olympian that they shouldn't have even tried or that they are less worthwhile as a person because they didn't get gold. Most Olympians don't get the gold medal; that's just how the world works. That doesn't make their time, efforts, journey, or intent any less meaningful or important.

Relying on external feedback or letting it overly impact how you view yourself is a trap. You don't always need to be achieving things to be worthwhile. You don't have to be perfect. You are important just because you exist.
